title: Homer in Hades: Ghosts of The Odyssey
author: Ben Potter
summary: Ben Potter, writing for Classical Wisdom, walks through Book XI of the Odyssey, the Nekyia, in which Odysseus descends to the underworld. He asks why Homer includes an episode that seems self-contained and concludes that it both enhances Odysseus's kleos as a man who has been to hell and back and lets the poet parade a series of cameos from the heroic dead. Potter recounts the blood-filled pit that lets the ghosts speak, the brief scene with Teiresias, and the meetings with Elpenor, Odysseus's mother, Agamemnon, Achilles and Ajax, and the damned figures Tityos, Tantalus and Sisyphus. He notes that the whole tale is narrated by Odysseus to the Phaiakians and that Alcinoos's praise of his honesty raises the old scholarly question of whether the wanderings are invented. Achilles's remark that he would rather be a thrall than king of the dead is read as repentance, a statement of the underworld's horror, or mere talk. The email wrapper adds a Halloween note and an event promotion, which are excluded.
points: Potter reads the Nekyia as serving two purposes, magnifying Odysseus's kleos and giving Homer room for a showcase of dead heroes.
Alcinoos's praise of Odysseus's honesty is ironic given his fame as a liar, which feeds the scholarly debate over whether his tales are fantasy.
The Agamemnon encounter sets virtuous Penelope against unfaithful Clytemnestra, shaping how the homecoming should be read.
Achilles's regret about his heroic choice is open to three readings, a sign of how Homer complicates the glory ethic.
quotes: Book XI, The Book of the Dead, or the Nekyia, is one of the more self-contained chapters in the Odyssey. So much so that it actually feels like it has been included for its own sake rather than any necessity of plot development.
Perhaps the more dominant reason for the descent is so Homer can indulge himself (and the reader) with a long line of impressive and entertaining cameos from dead heroes’ past.

Not only is the feat extraordinary in itself, but puts him in an elite group of death-defying heroes along with Heracles who, for one of his twelve labours, was forced to fetch Cerberus, the three-headed guard-dog, from the halls of Hades.

It should be stressed that this underworld excursion is narrated, not by Homer, but by Odysseus to Alcinoos and Arete, the king and queen of the Phaiakians, who are entertaining the shipwrecked hero following an unfortunate run-in with Poseidon.

This has led scholars to debate whether the stories he tells the Phaiakians (including those of the Cyclops, Circe, Calypso, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis) are pure fantasy made up on the spot by a mythomaniac.
This encounter is used to highlight the difference between the virtuous Penelope and the unfaithful Clytemnestra.

This seems to directly contradict his choice early in life when told he could either die young and famous as the hero of Troy, or old and unknown amongst his family. Scholastic interpretations state Achilles is either repenting his choice of war over peace, emphasising just how ghastly the underworld actually is, or simply talking rubbish.
